title: Chapter 101 – Tan Ruyan's Ledger
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Tan Ruyan]

Four months later.

Tan Ruyan keeps three ledgers, and only two of them are for sale.

The first she carries openly, in a satchel of waxed canvas, from the Tan stall on the Inner Court's market row to the counting room behind the shop: a plain accounting of reagents bought and sold, in her plain clerk's script, with the Sect's seal on the cover. The second lives in a locked drawer in her uncle's study, and records what the family tells the Sect it earns. The third she keeps in her head, and a small bone-bound book with no title, and it records what the family actually earns, and who pays, and why.

She is twenty. She was taught arithmetic before she was taught to breathe. At six she could estimate the price of a cart of Heartroot by the sound of the wheels. At twelve she saw that the Tan family's honest ledger and its true ledger were different books, and understood, with a child's severe clarity, that this was how a house stays alive. At fifteen she entered the Sect as a Servant and was told that she had talent. At seventeen she stood on the forty-first step of the Mountain Gate and was told she had more.

She does not think of it as talent. She thinks of it as listening.

This morning, in the gray before the market opens, she listens to a wall.

* * *

The wall is her uncle's study door, and what she hears behind it is her uncle's voice, low and tense, with a stranger's voice answering.

She does not stop. She does not slow. She passes along the corridor with her satchel on her shoulder and her eyes on the floor, a dutiful niece on her way to the counting room, and her ears do the rest. The shipment is late. The Treasury has asked for a delay. Yes, the same terms as always. And the, ah, special account? Is paid in the usual manner. A pause. A chair scrapes. I would remind you that the house cannot hold the account if the Cloud Peak Hall squeezes the license.

She is three paces beyond the door when the stranger's voice says a word she knows. She stops, as though to adjust her satchel. She does not turn.

The Registry sends its regards.

Her uncle laughs, a thin laugh, too bright. And mine to the Registry. Always.

She goes on down the corridor. In the counting room she sets the satchel on the table and sits, and takes out the bone-bound book, and writes a line in it that nobody else will ever read. Her hand does not shake. Her hand never shakes. That is what her teachers say of her, with admiration, and her mother with sorrow.

The house pays the Registry, she writes. Regularly. For years.

She closes the book and lays her palm on the cover. Her pulse is slow and steady. She feels, under it, a hard small coldness like a stone in a shoe.

So that is who reads the accounts.

* * *

Shen Yuhang stops her in the colonnade at noon.

He has not changed. He is as tall and pale and impeccably dressed as ever, with the jade pin in his hair and the fine sword at his hip, and his smile is exactly as courteous as it was before the Midsummer Trial. Only a faint new line has appeared at the corner of his mouth. It is the line of a man who smiles for a living, and has recently found it harder.

"Silver Leaf Tan."

"Silver Leaf Shen."

"You were at the Ring." He falls into step beside her, hands behind his back. "I saw you on the third bench. You did not cheer."

"I do not cheer at anything."

"A sensible habit." He studies the pillars as they pass. "Your family has a license difficulty, I understand. Three of them. A pity. The Hall has no wish to interfere with honest trade. But there are those on the floor who think the southern road should belong to a house of greater standing."

"The Cloud Peak Hall."

"I could not say." His smile does not change. "I only mention that I have a great respect for your family's discretion. For your uncle's especially. A man who keeps so many accounts open must find it hard to close them." He stops. "I would not like to see the Tan house make a poor friend."

She stops with him. The sun slants between the columns and lies in bars on the floor, and she stands in one of them with her satchel and her pin and her level dark eyes.

"Are you threatening me, Silver Leaf Shen?"

"I am advising you. As a colleague." His pale eyes are quite empty. "There is a difference, and it is not always visible from the inside."

"And the Gate Bearer?"

"What of him?"

"Is he also being advised?"

For the first time something moves in Shen's face. It is gone almost at once, but she sees it. Not anger. Something more like a man looking at a door he would very much like to see behind.

"I have nothing to say about the Gate Bearer," he says softly. "I have only a great deal to learn."

He inclines his head and walks on, his sword swinging, into the light.

* * *

The Tan family has been in the reagent trade for nine generations, and it has never forgotten that it began as a cart.

The cart is still there, in the hall of the great house in the town of Azure Cloud, mounted on the wall of the entry under a plaque. It is a plain two-wheeled thing of dark wood with a rusted axle, the sort a peddler drags along a mountain road. Below it, in neat gold characters, the founder's maxim: We carry what others will not, and we ask what it weighs.

Tan Ruyan stands before it at the family council, at the third bell, in her silver-edged gray, with her hands folded behind her.

She is the youngest of the seven at the table by twenty years. Her great-uncle Huai sits at the head, ninety years old, wrapped in a blanket, a cultivator who reached Foundation Late and stopped there, wise and near-deaf and as cunning as a snake in a drain. Beside him her uncle Boren, soft-handed and anxious. Her mother, thin and quiet. Four cousins. A clerk with a brush.

"The Cloud Peak Hall is squeezing us," says Boren. He is sweating. "Three licenses withdrawn since the Midsummer Trial. They say it is routine. It is not routine. They have bought the Treasury clerks, and they want to put us out."

"They want the reagent route," says great-uncle Huai, in a voice like paper. "The southern road. The Heartroot and the Moon-ash. It is the only thing in the Sect that pays."

"Then we lose it."

"We do not lose it. We find someone stronger." The old man's filmed eyes turn, with surprising precision, to his great-niece. "Ruyan. You have been quiet."

"I have been listening, Great-uncle."

"And?"

She draws a breath.

"There is a person in the Sect," she says, "who has the patronage of the Guard, the friendship of the Pill Hall, and the unconcealed hostility of the Cloud Peak Hall. He has a family Garden that is growing at the rate of one family a month, and no way to move its goods. He has a favor owed me from the Mountain Gate Trial, and a bud of Moon-ash lotus that came from his hand, which my uncle bought last winter at a very fair price."

"The Gate Bearer," says Boren, too quickly.

"The Gate Bearer."

"He is provisional. His standing could be struck at the next review."

"So could ours," says Ruyan. "If the Hall continues." She lets the sentence rest on the table. "I propose we invite him to the house. Not as a client. As a partner. The Tan name on the Garden's goods, the Garden's goods on the Tan road, and the Gate Bearer's protection on both."

The silence is long.

"His protection is worth what?" says one of the cousins.

"Very little, at present. A good deal more in two years." She keeps her voice level. "He has come out of a Founders' chamber with something that no one else in the Sect possesses. He has beaten the Cloud Peak heir in the Ring without a drop of Qi. He has the Guard's name staked on him, and the Guard has never been wrong in sixty years." She looks at her great-uncle. "I do not say he will win. I say he is the only person in the Sect who is not afraid of the Hall."

Huai is silent for a while. His breath rasps in the blanket.

"I will meet him," he says. "Bring him to the house at the next new moon. And Ruyan."

"Great-uncle?"

"Do not tell him what you want. Let him ask."

* * *

Her mother is waiting in the counting room when she returns from the council, with a pot of tea and a face like a shut window.

Tan Mei is fifty, and looks older. She was beautiful once, in a quiet way, and still holds her back as straight as a girl's. She sets down the pot without a word. She pours two cups.

"You did not tell your uncle," she says.

"No."

"You will not tell him?"

"I will tell him what he needs to know when he needs to know it."

"That is a cold thing to say about your father's brother."

"My father is dead, Mother. My uncle raised me." Ruyan takes the cup. "I know what I owe him. I know what I owe the house. I know what I owe the man who may be our only protection." She sips. "I am tired of owing."

Her mother is silent for a time. Her thin hands are folded on the table, and the knuckles are white.

"The Registry came to me once," she says at last. "Before you were born. A clerk, in a gray robe. He wanted to know the price of my silence. I said I had none. He said everyone has." Her voice is very low. "I learned what mine was. It was you."

Ruyan sets down the cup.

"I did not know that."

"You were not meant to." Tan Mei lifts her eyes. They are the same level dark eyes. "Your uncle pays them because I told him to. Seventeen years. It was the price of keeping you out of their book."

The room is very still.

"Then it was not Uncle Boren," says Ruyan slowly.

"It was both of us. It was the house." Her mother's mouth trembles. "If you give that page to anyone, you give them me as well."

* * *

She calls the favor in the Pill Hall, at the hour of the dusk bell, over a mortar of Heartroot.

He is working alone. The old Elder has gone to his dinner, and the dispensary is warm and dim, with a hundred little furnaces ticking down. Lin Jian sits at the long bench in his gray tunic, with the white jade tag at his throat and a faint pale scar showing at the collar where the sword went in. He has grown. It is not much, but she sees it: a breadth in the shoulder, a stillness in the hands. He is twenty-two, and moves like a man of thirty.

He does not look up when she enters.

"Silver Leaf Tan."

"Gate Bearer." She sits across the bench. "I would like to call the favor."

His pestle pauses. A trace of something crosses his face, and goes.

"Now?"

"At the next new moon. I wish you to come to my family's house in Azure Cloud." She watches his hands. "I wish you to meet my great-uncle. That is all. An introduction, and a cup of tea."

"That is a small favor."

"It is a favor that costs you nothing, and gains you nothing, and may change the whole of your Garden." She folds her hands. "I will not say more. My great-uncle has asked that I not."

He sets down the pestle. For a moment he studies her, with his steady dark gaze, and she has the unnerving sensation of being weighed on a scale that she cannot see.

"You are asking me to walk into a trap," he says, without heat.

"I am asking you to walk into a house."

"They are the same thing, sometimes."

"Yes." She does not look away. "They are. I will tell you this, because I think you would find it out and resent the delay. The Tan family is under pressure from the Cloud Peak Hall. We are looking for an ally. That is all my great-uncle has in mind. I will not insult you by saying it is not self-interest."

"You have not insulted me."

"I have not told you the rest."

"Which is?"

She hesitates. It is not like her. She feels the small cold stone in her shoe, the line in her bone-bound book. The house pays the Registry. Regularly. For years. She cannot say it here, in this room, where anyone might be listening. She cannot say it to a man who has just been named as the Registry's special wish.

"Which is," she says carefully, "that the house is not as clean as it looks. I will tell you when I can. I swear it on my favor."

He considers that for a long time.

"Very well," says Lin Jian. "At the new moon. I will come."

* * *

The Tan house in Azure Cloud is built around a courtyard of white gravel, with a pond in the middle and a single willow.

It is old, and it is quiet, and it smells faintly of incense and ledger-ink. Jian comes at dusk, on foot, with his hands in his sleeves, and Pebble riding invisibly under the cloak. He bows to the old man in the blanket, to the anxious uncle, to the silent mother. He drinks the tea. It is excellent. He says very little.

Ruyan sits at the foot of the table, at her great-uncle's right hand, and says less.

She watches the old man work.

It is a gentle process, and a merciless one. Huai talks about the weather. About the price of southern rice. About a cart he remembers from his boyhood, in which he rode a hundred miles to sell a sack of mushrooms and came back with a wife. He asks about the Garden's harvest. He asks about the clan's health. He listens, with his filmed eyes closed, as the Gate Bearer answers: seventy-one people, a plot by the river that floods, three roots among the new children, a herbalist girl in the Sutra Hall school.

"And the trade?" he asks. "How does the Garden sell?"

"Poorly," says Jian. "We have the Court's license for sales. We have the Pavilion's quota. We do not have a road."

"A road is a heavy thing to lack."

"It is."

"What would you do with one?"

"Feed people," says Jian simply. "And pay for a house."

Old Huai opens his eyes. He looks at the young man for a long moment, and then, to Ruyan's astonishment, he smiles. It is a small, dry, surprised smile, like a man who has found a coin in a sleeve he thought he had emptied.

"Boren," he says. "Bring the contract."

The contract has been drawn up for a week. Ruyan wrote half of it. Boren sets it on the table with a hand that trembles very slightly, and the clerk unrolls it, and the room waits.

There is a last page that she has not mentioned to him. Her great-uncle added it himself, in a shaking hand, the night before.

"There are fourteen bondsmen on the southern road," says Huai, as the clerk reaches it. "Drivers, porters, a cook. They are bound to the house for twenty years, by debt. Their children are born into the debt. It is an old practice, and I am ashamed of it." The filmed eyes open. "I would release them to the Garden. They have asked. They have heard that the Lin clan eats at one table. They do not understand it, but they would like to see."

Jian looks up.

"Fourteen."

"And their families. Thirty-one in all." The old man coughs. "They are good people. They know the road. They would train your guards and carry your goods. In return, the house is rid of a debt it never wished to hold, and the Garden gains hands."

"The Garden has seventy-one mouths and a plot that floods."

"Then it will have a hundred and two." Huai's thin lips twitch. "I am told it is a place that feeds people. I thought the Tan family might learn how."

Ruyan sees something happen in the Gate Bearer's face then. It is very slight. It is the look of a man who has been offered a coin and a hand in the same breath.

"I will take them," he says. "At the long table."

It is a good contract. It is more than fair. The Tan family will carry the Garden's goods on the southern road, under the Tan seal, at a fee of eleven in a hundred. The Garden will have the right to sell to any Tan factor at the posted price. The Tan family will supply four caravan guards and a driver, to be trained at the Garden by Old Hu. And in return...

"In return," says Huai, "the Gate Bearer will extend to the House of Tan the courtesy of his name."

Jian reads the clause. She sees his eyes move across it, slowly, and stop.

The courtesy of his name.

It is a gentle phrase. It means that when the Tan seal is stamped on a bale of Heartroot, so is the shadow of the Gate. It means that the House of Tan may say, to any magistrate or toll-keeper or Registry clerk: This is the Gate Bearer's road. And it means that anything done to the House of Tan is done, in some obscure but binding way, to him.

"You are asking me to be your shield," he says.

"I am asking you to be our friend," says the old man gently. "It is a matter of vocabulary."

"And if the Hall strikes you?"

"Then they strike you also. Which they intend to do in any case." Huai's voice is dry. "I would rather we were struck together. It halves the loneliness."

Jian is silent. Ruyan watches him, and she thinks, with a kind of tired clarity: He will say yes. He has no alternative. And he knows it. And he will say yes anyway, with his eyes open, because it is the best of the bad paths.

He signs.

He signs in a plain upright hand, with the Tan house's brush, and presses his thumb to the wax. The seal falls on the paper like a drop of blood.

"Good," says old Huai. He closes his eyes. "I am tired. Ruyan, see him out."

* * *

She walks him to the gate in the dark.

The night air is cool and smells of pond water.

She has not been alone in the courtyard in years. As a child she came here to sit under the willow and do sums in the dust, because it was the only place in the house with no one to ask what she was doing. It has not changed. The same gravel, the same pond, the same slow branches moving against the stars. She thinks, with a strange tenderness, that this is a thing she has loved without ever noticing. A garden is not a thing a person chooses. It is only a place where they were small.

She thinks of the Lin Garden, which she has seen only once, in the winter, from the road. A mess of sheds and terraces on a hill, loud with children, smelling of porridge and smoke. She had thought it ugly. She had thought it badly run. She had stood at the gate and seen a small woman in a blue robe counting people as they came in, one by one, with a tally-board, and giving each of them a bowl.

A house is the people it feeds, she thinks. I never knew that.

The courtyard is silver with moonlight. The willow shivers. A frog speaks once in the pond and is silent. Jian walks beside her with his hands in his sleeves, a step behind, which is a courtesy, and she is aware of it with a faint ache.

"You said you would tell me the rest," he says.

"I did."

"It is the Registry."

She stops. The moon throws her shadow long across the gravel.

"How do you know?"

"I do not know. I guessed." He is looking at the pond. "Your uncle's hand shook when he set down the contract. It was not fear of me. It was fear of something that would see it."

She says nothing. The wind moves in the willow. She feels a muscle in her jaw tighten.

"I keep three ledgers," she says at last, very low. "One for the Sect. One for the family. One for the truth. The third says that the House of Tan has paid the Registry for seventeen years. Not tribute. Not a tax. A standing monthly sum, from my uncle's own account, to a number I cannot trace." She breathes. "I found the entry the year I became a Servant. I thought it was a mistake. I have thought so for six years."

"And now?"

"And now I think the house has been paying the Registry for seventeen years to keep something safe. And I think that something is me." Her voice does not break. "And I think the contract you signed tonight is the first thing the Tan house has done in seventeen years that the Registry did not ask for."

Jian turns his head and looks at her.

"They will know."

"Yes."

"They will punish your uncle."

"Yes."

"And you?"

"I do not know." She meets his eyes. "I have the page. In the bone-bound book. The ledger entries, seventeen years of them, in my uncle's hand. I could give it to you. It would show where the money goes. It might show who receives it. It would also show that Tan Boren, who raised me, has been a Registry paymaster since before I could walk."

Neither of them speaks. The moon slides behind a cloud, and the courtyard darkens.

"I have never given up a family secret," says Ruyan. "I have been taught since I was a child that it is the only sin the Tan house does not forgive. That a ledger is a trust."

"And now?"

"And now I am standing in my own courtyard, at midnight, with a man I owe a favor, deciding whether to burn my uncle." She takes the little book from her sleeve. It is warm from her body. She holds it in her hand, a small bone-bound rectangle with no title. "I called your favor for an introduction. I think I did it so that I would have a reason to stand here."

He waits.

Say it, she thinks. Give him the page, or put the book away. One or the other. There is no third thing.

She opens the book. She turns it to the entry, and tears out the leaf, one clean stroke along the binding, and holds it out in the moonlight between two fingers.

"Take it," says Tan Ruyan. "Before I change my mind."
